claims.text: The initial sub-10 nm equiatomic Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles are a single-phase solid solution.
The sluggish-diffusion assumption breaks down above 600 K in sub-10 nm Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles.
Surface-energy-driven segregation and Ostwald ripening dominate the structural evolution above this threshold.
A high surface-to-volume ratio lowers the kinetic barrier for atomic exchange.
The nanoparticles undergo rapid phase separation rather than entropy-stabilized kinetic arrest.
The smallest particles are selectively lost through vaporization or coalescence.
The proposed intervention is heating the particles in vacuum from room temperature to 1000 K.
Surface diffusion pathways and surface-energy gradients override bulk configurational-entropy stabilization at the nanoscale.
At elevated temperature, the thermodynamic driving force for reducing surface and interfacial energy exceeds the kinetic barrier associated with sluggish bulk diffusion.
High surface energy facilitates rapid surface diffusion and atomic exchange in sub-10 nm particles.
Low-surface-energy elements such as Au and Pt segregate to the surface or core.
Ostwald ripening proceeds through dissolution of smaller particles and redeposition onto larger particles.
Ripening, evaporation, and coalescence produce loss of small particles and morphology changes such as faceting or aggregate formation.
Heating will produce distinct elemental or binary-rich domains.
Heating will significantly reduce the number of particles smaller than 5 nm.
High configurational entropy and sluggish bulk diffusion are expected by the baseline model to preserve a single-phase solid solution up to 1000 K.
The proposed surface-dominated mechanism is limited to particles below 10 nm and may not apply above 50 nm, where bulk sluggish diffusion remains dominant.
The crossover temperature depends on constituent surface energies and defect populations.
In-situ SAXS, mass spectrometry, EDS/EDX, and XRD are proposed to distinguish particle-size evolution, vaporization, compositional segregation, and phase separation.
Retention of a single-phase structure with no significant size or composition change, together with phase-separation rates no faster than bulk, would falsify the hypothesis.
